## Negative Torque Can Help a Positive Outcome {#sec-lay-ch13}

## A Concrete Picture

Imagine a club receiving a force through its moving grip while a couple opposes
its rotation. The couple can remove rotational power at the chosen grip point
while the force supplies more power than the couple removes. The club can gain
kinetic energy. No energy is created by the minus sign: two physical inputs have
different effects, and their sum decides the instantaneous energy change.

A second question is harder. Could a schedule containing an opposing moment
produce a better later delivery than a schedule without it? Possibly, because
the moment changes the evolving state and the work subsequently done by other
inputs. That outcome requires a controlled comparison. It does not follow from
negative torque, apparent wrist lag, or the existence of a reaction force.

![Power Signs for One Conjugate Rotational Channel: Club-Side Moment Uses Absolute Club Rate; an Internal Joint Pair Uses Relative Rate.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_torque_power_quadrants.svg){#fig-lay-torque-quadrants width=94% fig-alt="Four quadrants show positive power when a torque and its conjugate angular rate have the same sign, and negative power when their signs differ. The footer distinguishes absolute club rate from relative joint rate."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Name the Torque and Its Conjugate Velocity

For a single rotational power channel, $P=\tau\dot\theta$. The word
*conjugate* means that this torque and this rate belong to the same virtual-work
pair. A club-side free moment uses the club's absolute angular velocity in the
declared inertial observer. An internal wrist moment acting between club and
forearm has an equal and opposite reaction on the forearm. Their combined
rotational joint power uses the **relative** angular velocity; the subscript
$\mathrm m$ below denotes the moment contribution:

$$
P_{\mathrm{club,m}}=\tau\omega_c,\qquad
P_{\mathrm{arm,m}}=-\tau\omega_a,\qquad
P_{\mathrm{joint}}=\tau(\omega_c-\omega_a).
$$

For a manufactured planar example, let $\tau=-2$ N m on the club,
$\omega_c=3$ rad/s and $\omega_a=5$ rad/s. The moment supplies $-6$ W to the
club and $+10$ W to the arm; the pair supplies $+4$ W. Calling this a
negative-power joint merely because the club moment is negative would be wrong.
With coordinates $(\theta_a,\beta)$, where $\beta=\theta_c-\theta_a$, this
internal motor has generalized force $(0,\tau)$ and power $\tau\dot\beta$.
With absolute coordinates $(\theta_a,\theta_c)$ it has generalized force
$(-\tau,\tau)$. Both
descriptions give the same total power.

In three dimensions use the full dot product
$\mathbf M\cdot\boldsymbol\omega$, or
$\mathbf M\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega_c-\boldsymbol\omega_a)$ for the
rotational joint pair, with vectors expressed in one common frame. A negative
swing-normal component alone does not determine the full dot product. Neither
Euler-angle derivatives nor anatomical labels can be substituted for angular
velocity components without their coordinate mapping. Reversing a scalar axis
reverses both conjugate signs and leaves power unchanged.

### Follow Power Across a Declared Boundary

For a rigid club before impact, choose an inertial observer and a material grip
point $H$. Reduce all hand contacts to a resultant force $\mathbf F$ and moment
$\mathbf M_H$ about that point. If the only other external action is uniform
gravity, the kinetic-energy balance is

$$
\dot T_c=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_H
+\mathbf M_H\cdot\boldsymbol\omega_c
+m\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf v_C,
$$

where $C$ is the club's center of mass. Other physical loads require their own
power terms. If gravitational potential is included in stored energy instead,
gravity moves to the left side; it is not counted again on the right.

For a flexible club, include shaft strain energy and distinguish dissipation
from recoverable storage. The exact input is the sum of contact forces dotted
with their actual contact velocities, together with any contact-moment powers.
A single rigid wrench formula needs compatible rigid motion; deformation or
slip can add terms. Shaft release redistributes stored club energy. It is not a
second external input to a boundary already enclosing the entire shaft.
Likewise, *inertial coupling* describes the equations' redistribution of motion;
it is not an additional energy supply alongside the complete physical balance.

Negative instantaneous power means the selected channel removes energy at that
instant. Work is its time integral. A short negative interval does not determine
the sign of work over the entire downswing, total club energy, or final speed.

### A Moment Can Change Sign When Its Reference Point Changes

Keep the observer fixed and let $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_C-\mathbf r_H$. Rigid
velocity and moment transport give

$$
\mathbf v_C=\mathbf v_H+\boldsymbol\omega_c\times\mathbf r,\qquad
\mathbf M_C=\mathbf M_H-\mathbf r\times\mathbf F.
$$

The complete wrench power is the same about $H$ and $C$, although its force and
moment parts differ. Take $\mathbf r=(0,1,0)$ m,
$\mathbf v_H=(2,0,0)$ m/s, $\boldsymbol\omega_c=(0,0,3)$ rad/s,
$\mathbf F=(10,0,0)$ N and $\mathbf M_H=(0,0,-2)$ N m. Then
$\mathbf v_C=(-1,0,0)$ m/s and $\mathbf M_C=(0,0,8)$ N m. At the grip,
power is $20-6=14$ W; at the center it is $-10+24=14$ W. The reported moment
changes from negative to positive without changing the physical force system.
These are instantaneous manufactured values, not a golfer's measurements.

Only a pure couple, with zero resultant force, has reference-independent moment.
For general hand loading, always name the moment point. Changing the inertial
observer is a different operation: body power can change with observer even
when reference-point transport within one observer preserves it.

### What Two Hands Add

Let $L$ and $T$ denote the lead and trail hands. At the grip midpoint, use the
archive's convention for contact separation and differential force:
$\mathbf d=\mathbf r_T-\mathbf r_L$ and differential force as
$\mathbf F_d=(\mathbf F_L-\mathbf F_T)/2$. The force-generated moment is
$\mathbf M_{F,H}=-\mathbf d\times\mathbf F_d$. Any free moments applied
by the hands must be added separately. Large opposing forces can therefore
produce a substantial moment despite a small resultant.

Holding the forces fixed while reversing $\mathbf d$ reverses this moment;
collapsing finite-force lever arms removes it. Neither operation proves that a
new forward swing will have reversed or vanished total torque. A changed grip
geometry changes the constraints and their reaction forces, may require a new
compatible initial state, and need not eliminate free moments. Rotating the
entire force system and its measuring axis together preserves the scalar
projection. Changing their relative geometry is the relevant intervention.

Ideal maintained contact can transfer energy between bodies while doing zero
net work on the complete system. For stationary holonomic constraints with
$J\dot q=0$, total constraint power is
$\lambda^{\mathsf T}J\dot q=0$, where $q$ contains generalized coordinates,
$J$ is the constraint Jacobian and $\lambda$ contains the multipliers producing
generalized reaction $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$. One-sided club contact power need not be
zero. Prescribed moving supports, compliance, friction and impacts require
their own accounting; this ideal cancellation is not a universal contact law.

### Three Model Results Answer Three Different Questions

The pinned [two-hand archive analysis](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/chapters/_ch05_two_hand_wrench.qmd)
reconstructs an archived project simulation at achieved states. Its zero-command
table is **pointwise**, not one torque-free forward swing. The late negative
couple is a contact-force reaction with current commanded wrist moments and
the designated damping removed.
Earlier commands helped create the states being evaluated.

Crucially, this archive does not show a positive-power boost from that late
couple. Reconstructed contact-force power, the sum
$\mathbf F_L\cdot\mathbf v_L+\mathbf F_T\cdot\mathbf v_T$ on the club,
is negative at about 85% of samples
inside its approximately 88 ms negative-couple interval, with about $-149$ J
of integrated contact-force work. The archive's separate power columns have a
reported pointwise discrepancy, reaching about 73 W; interval agreement does
not remove that limitation. These are model records, not participant data or
proof of a speed-improving strategy.

The separate [forward constrained test](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/chapters/_ch05b_forward_two_hand.qmd)
uses two planar arms and a floating rigid club. Its zero-command branch at
0.200 s retains a negative force-generated couple for the next 50 ms. A later
branch changes sign before its 50 ms window ends. This demonstrates finite,
state-dependent persistence in that model. It neither reproduces the WSCG
trajectory nor establishes a benefit in speed, human muscle behavior or impact
delivery. Reported numerical projection corrections also remain part of its
error assessment, not physical work.

The [uncertainty and control comparison](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/chapters/_ch06d_uncertainty_control.qmd)
uses a different planar moving-base, two-hand, flexible-club model with bounded
actuators. Among eight sampled schedules and six held-out parameter draws,
`early_restrain` has the highest sampled 10th-percentile endpoint speed, about
4.706 m/s. Its mean planar face/path error proxy exceeds that of `late_drive`.
All eight candidates are nondominated under five objectives: this speed
quantile, mean face/path error, upper-tail hand force, squared-torque effort
and speed dispersion. Nondominated means no other sampled candidate is at least
as good in every objective and better in one.
The endpoint is a fixed 0.24 s delivery time, with no ball collision. These
results describe a finite synthetic comparison, not a continuous optimum,
population reliability bound, or calibrated human swing. The schedule name
alone does not establish the sign of its work throughout the trajectory.

**Model Result:** A negative contact moment can persist without current
command, and a selected restraining schedule can perform well under a separate
model's objectives. Persistence and performance are different findings.

**Human Evidence:** Morrison and colleagues studied kinematic variability with
uncontrolled-manifold analysis; that citation does not establish wrist EMG or
identify a passive grip couple [@morrison2016]. Nesbit combined recorded motion
with a full-body and flexible-club model to estimate kinetics. Its wrist motion
was kinematically driven, and its hand representation was simplified; inferred
interface loads are not isolated muscle measurements [@nesbit2005kinematic].

**Hypothesis:** In some feasible states, an opposing distal contribution may
improve later delivery by changing geometry and the subsequent allocation of
work. The useful states, mechanisms and tradeoffs remain to be established.

**Practical Interpretation:** Ask for the body, reference point, conjugate
velocity, work interval and objective before judging a torque sign.

### How to Test Whether Restraint Helped

Start with a complete copied state: positions, velocities, actuator activation
and any elastic or controller memory included in the model. Declare whether
the intervention removes a command, a finite realized torque, damping, or a
contact mode. With smooth finite forces and the same constraints, removing a
torque does not instantaneously change velocity. It changes the applicable
acceleration and subsequent evolution; a particular acceleration component
need not change. Activation dynamics may delay the effect of command removal.
An impulsive event or changed contact constraint is a different intervention.

Integrate each branch with its own evolving reactions and power balance.
Compare the same declared endpoint: fixed time, a registered delivery event,
or a modeled impact. If an event moves or becomes unreachable, report that
instead of comparing unlike states. Subtract branch outcomes to estimate a
conditional effect within the declared model. A pointwise torque decomposition
is not a decomposition of separately integrated future trajectories.

For a strategy comparison, state what remains matched: initial state, proximal
control policy, available actuator capacity, task requirements and uncertainty
draws. Identical torque schedules do not imply equal work once velocities
differ. Reoptimization asks whether another feasible route can substitute for
restraint; it changes the question from removing one input in a fixed policy.
Neither comparison should silently receive the other's interpretation.

Descriptions such as arms driving while wrists regulate, or a phase-dependent
reversal of those roles, are hypotheses about measured force and moment
allocation. Continuous loading can change actuator and elastic history even
at similar poses. Compare those proposals through matched tasks, bilateral
loads and work, rather than assigning a biological role from one torque curve.

An early opposing phase might delay release and change later force directions;
it might also increase proximal work, violate load limits or leave inadequate
time. There need not be an interior optimum or a useful restraint interval.
Map feasible outcomes before claiming an optimum region. Keep the finite
candidate comparison distinct from any newly proposed search.

### Negative Work Needs a Destination

For a torsional spring with relative deflection $\beta$, torque
$-k\beta$ gives relative power $-k\beta\dot\beta=-\dot U$, where
$U=k\beta^2/2$. Absorbed mechanical energy is stored and may later return.
A viscous damper instead gives power $-c\dot\beta^2\le0$ for $c\ge0$.
The same instantaneous power sign can therefore accompany recoverable storage,
transfer to another body, or dissipation. Select the actual mechanism and
boundary before naming a loss.

At a human joint, a net moment and relative rate cannot uniquely separate
muscle fibers, tendons, passive tissues and opposing muscle groups. EMG supplies
an activation-related signal, not a unique force or work measurement. Bilateral
wrench sensing, registered contact geometry, shaft measurements and a calibrated
model can constrain the explanation; their uncertainty and unresolved internal
loads must remain visible.

### Reader Lab: Audit a “Negative Helps” Claim

Reproduce the $-6$, $+10$ and $+4$ W joint example, then the two equivalent
$14$ W wrench reductions. Explain why neither calculation establishes a
future speed benefit. Plot torque with its conjugate rate, instantaneous power
and cumulative work for the selected interval. Add all other physical inputs
and stored-energy changes, and inspect the closure residual.

Next specify a feasible copied-state intervention and the future outcome being
compared. Separate evidence for moment sign, energy transfer, persistence and
performance. A failure of the negative sign to persist would limit a persistence
hypothesis; a worse feasible outcome would limit a strategy claim. A human
measurement inconsistent with the predicted wrench would challenge transfer
of that mechanism to golfers. None of these tests is replaced by an attractive
sequence plot.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The brake metaphor suggests an independent wheel. A swing has moving supports,
coupled coordinates, elastic storage and several objectives. Even the sign of
the reported club moment needs a point and axis; a favorable planar result
can coexist with an unfavorable face orientation or load.

“Passive” must name the channel left uncommanded. Zero current command does
not mean zero force, zero prior work, zero activation or biological relaxation.
The useful question is how a specified action changes a feasible trajectory
and its energy balance, with evidence strong enough to support that scope.

with the distinct archive, forward and uncertainty studies above. Their model
